name: Picture Logic
intro: A short path through Picture Logic: how the number clues work, then the overlap and edge methods that solve almost every line.

lessons.title: Reading the clues
lessons.summary: Each Picture Logic clue lists the runs of filled squares in its row or column, in order. Learn to read the clues and fill your first lines.
lessons.wrap: Runs in order, with gaps between. Next: a quick rules check.

steps.text:
Every row and column has a clue. Each number is a run of filled squares in that line, in order, with at least one empty square between runs.

The top row’s clue is 2 2: a run of two, a gap, then another run of two. Fill every line to match its clue and a picture appears.
Here’s the same puzzle, empty. The second row’s clue is 8, and the row is 8 squares wide.
steps.prompt: Tap all eight squares of the second row.
steps.wrong: Stay in the second row from the top.
steps.done: A clue as long as the line fills it completely.

steps.prompt: A row’s clue is 3 1. What does it mean?
options: A run of three, then a gap, then a run of one
steps.explain: A run of three, at least one empty square, then a run of one, in that order.

steps.prompt: What does a clue of 0 mean?
steps.explain: The whole line is empty. Cross it out straight away.

units.name: Rules check
units.blurb: Four questions on the rules. Pass to unlock the methods.

lessons.title: Picture Logic rules check
lessons.summary: Test your Picture Logic rules: reading row and column clues, the order of runs, the gaps between them, and lines that are full or empty.
lessons.wrap: Rules check passed. Now for the methods.

steps.prompt: A clue says 2 4. Which comes first along the line?
steps.explain: Runs are always in the order the clue lists them: left to right in a row, top to bottom in a column.

steps.prompt: Can two runs in the same line touch?
options: No, there’s always at least one empty square between them
steps.explain: No. Otherwise they’d be one longer run.

steps.prompt: The row second from the bottom has a clue of 8. Tap all its squares.
steps.wrong: Count up two rows from the bottom.

steps.prompt: In a line of 8, a clue of 1 4 1 needs 1 + 4 + 1 squares plus two gaps. How many ways can it fit?
steps.explain: 1 + 4 + 1 + 2 gaps = 8, the whole line. When a clue adds up to the line’s length, there’s only one way to fill it.

units.name: Solving methods
units.blurb: The overlap method and the edge method.

lessons.title: The overlap method
lessons.summary: Push a run as far left as it goes, then as far right: the squares it covers both times must be filled. Learn the overlap method on a real puzzle.
lessons.wrap: Left, right, overlap. Start every puzzle with the biggest clues. Next: the edge method.

steps.text:
The first column’s clue is 7, in a column of 8. Pushed to the top, the run covers squares 1 to 7 (highlighted). Pushed to the bottom, it covers 2 to 8.

Squares 2 to 7 are filled either way, so you can fill them now. That’s the overlap.

steps.prompt: Tap the six squares of the first column that must be filled.
steps.wrong: Not the very top or the very bottom: those depend on where the run sits.

steps.text: It works with several runs too. The top row is 3 3. Pushed left: squares 1–3 and 5–7. Pushed right: 2–4 and 6–8.
steps.prompt: Tap the four squares of the top row where each run overlaps itself.
steps.wrong: Each run of three shares two squares between its left and right positions.

steps.text: The biggest overlap of all: the sixth row is 1 4 1. That’s 1 + 4 + 1 squares plus two gaps: exactly 8. There’s only one way to fit it.
steps.prompt: Tap every filled square of the sixth row.
steps.wrong: One square, a gap, four squares, a gap, one square.
steps.done: When a clue adds up to the line, the whole line is solved.

lessons.title: The edge method
lessons.summary: A filled square at the edge of a Picture Logic grid must start a run. Learn the edge method and how crossing out empty squares helps.
lessons.wrap: Edges start runs, and crosses mark what’s empty. Work rows, then columns, then rows again, and the picture appears.

steps.text:
From the overlap, the second column now has its top square filled (highlighted). Its clue is 2 1 2.

A filled square touching the edge must be the start of the first run. Here that run is 2 long, so it covers the top two squares, and the square after it must be empty.

steps.prompt: Tap the square that completes the second column’s first run.
steps.wrong: The run of 2 starts at the top, so it goes one square further down.

steps.text: A run of 2 is now finished, so the next square must stay empty. On the real board you’d cross it out.
steps.prompt: Tap the square that must be empty.
steps.wrong: It’s straight after the finished run.
steps.done: Crosses are just notes, but they make the next step easier to see.

steps.text: The third column has the same top square filled, and its clue is 2 4.
steps.prompt: What does the edge method tell you about the third column?
options: Its top two squares are filled and the third is empty
steps.explain: Same as before: the first run is 2 long and starts at the edge. Every square you fill in a column is new information for its row, and the other way round.
